name: Inner City Parish Church of the Assumption
description: The Inner City Parish Church of the Assumption sits at the Pest end of Elisabeth Bridge, which was designed as an arch so the church could stay. A Gothic hall church that served as a mosque under Ottoman rule, it still has a mihrab, and Roman fort remains were found beneath it in 2014 to 2016.

children.text: The Inner City Parish Church of the Assumption, in Hungarian the Belvárosi Nagyboldogasszony Főplébánia, stands at Március 15. tér 2 in Budapest's fifth district. It is a Roman Catholic parish church of the Archdiocese of Esztergom-Budapest, and its own website has a section for visitors as well as for parishioners. The parish gives the church's age as more than 950 years, although the date of the first Christian church is unknown.

What you see today is mostly a Gothic hall church with three aisles and an ambulatory, built from around 1370 to 1490 under King Louis the Great and later kings. The south tower dates from the reign of Matthias. Visit Hungary records that Matthias was elected king here in 1458 and Ulászló in 1490, and that the church's earliest layers go back to Roman times: a renovation in 2014 to 2016 uncovered remains of the Roman fort Contra Aquincum.

During Ottoman rule, from 1541, the church was used as a mosque, and a mihrab, the prayer niche, still survives in the wall. After the Ottomans were expelled in 1686 only the Gothic sanctuary was usable. Archbishop György Széchényi paid for a vault and conservation work on the nave in the following decades. The result is a building where Gothic, Ottoman and Baroque elements sit side by side.

The church is closely tied to Pest's public life. Count István Széchenyi lay in state here in 1860, Franz Joseph took the royal oath in front of the church in 1867, though sources differ on whether this was before or after his coronation, and Visit Hungary says Franz Liszt was a frequent guest and occasional conductor between 1858 and 1871. When Elisabeth Bridge was planned in the 1890s, demolishing the church was considered; instead the bridge was designed as an arch so the church could stay.

Look for the sanctuary vault, painted by Imre Steindl in 1889, and the 14th-century Madonna fresco found behind the main altar in 2010. The church was heavily damaged in 1944, losing its high altar and a tower spire; the new spire was finished by 1957. The 2014 to 2016 excavations ended when Cardinal Péter Erdő blessed the church on 14 August 2016. The parish site also mentions lookouts in the Baroque towers, which opened to visitors in 2020.
Good to know
This is an active parish. The parish website, belvarosiplebania.hu, has the current visiting arrangements, Mass times, tower lookout information and a virtual tour.
Groups should register in advance with the parish, which lists a separate contact for guided visits.
Stand on the bridge side and look at how Elisabeth Bridge curves around the church, which the Visit Hungary history describes as deliberate.
Look for the mihrab inside, a reminder of the Ottoman period.

historyIntro: The Inner City Parish Church of the Assumption has a history of more than 950 years, according to its parish. It has been a Gothic hall church, a mosque and a Baroque-restored parish church, and excavations in 2014 to 2016 found Roman fort remains beneath it.

historySections.heading: From the first church to the Gothic hall

children.text: The parish says the church was already standing in 1046, when Saint Gellért was martyred at the Pest ferry, though the date of the first Christian church is unknown; Visit Hungary instead says Gellért was buried here in 1046 before his remains were moved. The parish records that, according to a canon's chronicle, Louis of Thuringia likely became engaged to the future Saint Elizabeth of Hungary here in 1211. The Mongol invasion destroyed the original church in 1242. Under King Louis the Great, from about 1370, a new three-aisled Gothic hall church with an ambulatory was built, and the south tower dates from the reign of Matthias. Visit Hungary records that Matthias was elected king here in 1458 and Ulászló in 1490.

From 1541, under Ottoman rule, the church was used as a mosque, and a mihrab, the prayer niche, remains in the wall. The parish says it was one of the few churches in Pest that stayed in Catholic hands during the period. After the Ottomans were expelled in 1686, only the Gothic sanctuary was usable. Between 1686 and 1725, Archbishop György Széchényi funded a vault and conservation work on the nave. Over the following centuries the building was restored several times, usually by leading architects working in the style of their day, which is why Visit Hungary says its façade and interior mix styles from different eras.

historySections.heading: A civic landmark, war damage and excavation

children.text: Count István Széchenyi's lying-in-state was held here in 1860, and in 1867 Franz Joseph took the royal oath before the church. In 1889 Imre Steindl painted the sanctuary vault. In the 1890s demolition was considered when Elisabeth Bridge was planned, but the bridge was designed as an arch so the church could stay. Bombing in 1944 damaged the vaults, roof and walls, destroyed the high altar and one tower spire; the new spire was finished by 1957. In 2010 a 14th-century Madonna fresco was uncovered behind the main altar, and in 2014 to 2016 excavations found remains of the Roman fort Contra Aquincum. Cardinal Erdő blessed the church on 14 August 2016.

stories.title: An engagement in 1211

children.text: The parish's history says that, according to a canon's chronicle, Louis of Thuringia likely became engaged to Saint Elizabeth of Hungary in this church in 1211. Visit Hungary similarly states that the engagement of the four-year-old Elisabeth was held here.
The parish itself hedges the claim with the word likely, so it is best read as a recorded tradition from a chronicle rather than a certain fact.

name: Deák Square Lutheran Church
description: A plain neoclassical Lutheran church at Deák Ferenc tér 4, designed by Mihály Pollack and built between 1799 and 1808, with a Doric-pilastered façade rebuilt by József Hild in 1856. It is an active Lutheran parish church and stands next to the Evangelical National Museum.

children.text: The Deák Square Lutheran Church, in Hungarian the Deák téri evangélikus templom, stands at Deák Ferenc tér 4 in Budapest's fifth district. It is a Lutheran, or Evangelical, parish church and still hosts services and concerts. A We Love Budapest listing calls it the city's oldest and largest Protestant church, and notes that the Evangelical National Museum operates next to it.

The architect was Mihály Pollack, one of the main builders of neoclassical Pest. A We Love Budapest article on Pollack says he designed the church in the late 1790s with master builder János Krausz and took over the project after Krausz died. Hungarian Wikipedia gives the construction period as 1799 to 1808. The building was not used as a church at once: from July 1809 to spring 1811 it served as a military clothing store, and it was consecrated at Pentecost in 1811.

The exterior is deliberately plain. The façade has four Doric pilasters, a cornice with triglyphs and metopes, and a triangular pediment, under a large convex metal roof. József Hild rebuilt the main façade in 1856. Pollack's design was compact and unadorned, which the We Love Budapest article says sparked debate at a time when late Baroque still shaped architecture.

Inside is a single rectangular nave with a double gallery, completed in 1820. Pollack designed the altar, which carries a painting by Ferenc Lochbichler based on Raphael's Transfiguration, and Lőrinc Dunaiszky made the pulpit and the red marble baptismal font. The church was changed over time: in 1875 the classicist tower was removed for structural reasons and the barrel vault was replaced with a coffered ceiling.

In the courtyard, two bronze reliefs commemorate the 500th anniversary of Luther's birth and the 300th anniversary of Bach's birth. A marble plaque on the façade records that Lajos Kossuth had his sons baptised here. The church also sheltered many people during the great flood of 1838.
Good to know
This is an active parish church. Check the parish website, deakter.hu, for services, music events and when visitors can enter.
The Evangelical National Museum is next door but is a separate institution; check its own site for opening times and tickets.
Walk around to the courtyard side to see the bronze reliefs of Luther and Bach mentioned in the Hungarian Wikipedia article.
Compare the plain façade with the more ornate churches elsewhere in the city centre.

historyIntro: The Lutheran church on Deák tér was built between 1799 and 1808 to designs by Mihály Pollack, and consecrated only in 1811 after serving briefly as a military store. Its façade was rebuilt by József Hild in 1856.

historySections.heading: Building a Lutheran church in Pest

children.text: Mihály Pollack designed the church in the late 1790s, working with master builder János Krausz and taking over the project after Krausz died, according to a We Love Budapest article on Pollack. Hungarian Wikipedia gives the construction period as 1799 to 1808. The church was finished before it could be used for worship: from July 1809 to spring 1811 it served as a military clothing store. It was consecrated at Pentecost in 1811, and the double gallery was completed in 1820. Pollack also designed the altar, which carries a painting by Ferenc Lochbichler after Raphael's Transfiguration.

historySections.heading: Floods, new façade and altered interior

children.text: During the great flood of 1838 the church sheltered many people. József Hild rebuilt the main façade in 1856, giving it four Doric pilasters, a triglyph and metope cornice and a triangular pediment; Károly Benkó directed construction work from 1867. The church was damaged in a bombardment associated with Hentzi, as Hungarian Wikipedia puts it; the article gives no year. In 1875 the classicist tower was removed for structural reasons, and the barrel vault was replaced with a coffered ceiling.

Hungarian Wikipedia says the church was also damaged in the Second World War and during the construction of the M2 metro line. A small computer-controlled chime was installed around 2000, and the most recent exterior renovation mentioned in the article took place in 2003. In the courtyard two bronze reliefs commemorate the 500th anniversary of Luther's birth and the 300th anniversary of Bach's birth, and the Evangelical National Museum operates next to the church.

name: Saint Emeric Cistercian Church
description: The Buda Cistercian Saint Emeric Church at Villányi út 25 is a neo-Baroque parish church consecrated in 1938 and designed by Gyula Wälder. Its twin towers face Feneketlen Lake in Szentimreváros, and it stands beside the Cistercian school; the parish has again been run by the order since 1989.

children.text: The Buda Cistercian Saint Emeric Church, in Hungarian the Budai ciszterci Szent Imre-templom, stands at Villányi út 25 in Szentimreváros, part of Budapest's eleventh district, Újbuda. It is a Roman Catholic parish church of the Archdiocese of Esztergom-Budapest, dedicated to Saint Emeric, and the parish has again been run by the Cistercians since 1989. The parish office is at Himfy utca 9.

The church was designed by the architect and university professor Gyula Wälder for the Cistercian order. Hungarian Wikipedia gives its style as neo-Baroque and says it was built in 1938, the jubilee year of Saint Emeric, and consecrated that year by Cardinal-Primate Jusztinián Serédi. Wikidata gives the date as 6 November 1938. It belongs to a larger complex: the Cistercians settled in Buda in 1912, and the Feneketlen Lake article says Wälder planned a church, monastery, gymnasium and boarding school near the lake, with construction beginning in 1927.

The site relates closely to the lake. According to Hungarian Wikipedia, Feneketlen Lake began as a clay pit worked for a brickworks, and its origin is usually dated to 1877; the brickworks closed in 1889. When the surrounding park was landscaped in 1958 to 1960, the designer Mihály Mőcsényi aimed to make the church's twin towers visible as a reflection on the water, turning that view into a landmark of the district. The church and the Budai Ciszterci Szent Imre Gimnázium stand on the north side of the lake, across Villányi út.

Hungarian Wikipedia lists a main altar with a painting, a pulpit, side altars, a painted coffered ceiling, porcelain Stations of the Cross, a statue of Mary and a baptismal chapel with the Batthyány-Strattmann baptistery. The interior was renovated in 1972 to 1975 and the exterior in 1976 to 1979, and the façade and roof were reconstructed in 2019 to 2020, when the towers also received clocks. The parish website lists a sanctuary renovation project for 2026.
Good to know
This is an active parish church. Check the parish website, szentimre.hu, for Mass times, visiting arrangements and the current renovation work on the sanctuary.
Walk to the lake first and look back across the water at the twin towers, the view the park designer planned.
Feneketlen Lake is a short walk away; Hungarian Wikipedia describes the park around it, with an open-air stage, a running track and sculptures.
The church is beside an active Cistercian school, so show consideration for pupils in the surrounding streets.

historyIntro: The church at Villányi út 25 was built for the Cistercian order and consecrated in 1938. It is part of a Cistercian complex planned by Gyula Wälder on the north side of Feneketlen Lake.

children.text: According to Hungarian Wikipedia's article on Feneketlen Lake, the Cistercian order settled in Buda in 1912. The architect Gyula Wälder designed a complex with a church, monastery, gymnasium and boarding school near the shore of the lake, and construction began in 1927. The lake itself had formed from a clay pit, with its origin usually dated to 1877, after a brickworks that closed in 1889. The church and the Budai Ciszterci Szent Imre Gimnázium stand on the north side of the lake, across Villányi út.

The church itself was built in 1938, the jubilee year of Saint Emeric, to the neo-Baroque design of Wälder. Cardinal-Primate Jusztinián Serédi consecrated it; Wikidata gives the date as 6 November 1938. When the lakeside park was landscaped in 1958 to 1960, the designer Mihály Mőcsényi aimed to make the church's twin towers visible as a reflection on the lake's surface. The parish has been run by the Cistercians again since 1989.

Hungarian Wikipedia records an interior renovation in 1972 to 1975 and an exterior renovation in 1976 to 1979. The façade and roof were reconstructed in 2019 to 2020, and the towers received clocks. The parish website lists a sanctuary renovation project for 2026, so visitors should expect that parts of the church may be affected by works and should check with the parish.
